doc.title: Ruth Brown interviewed by Michael Woods, Scottsdale, Arizona, March 4, 1995

title: Rhythm and blues versus gospel; the moaner's bench
summary: Brown agrees R&B and gospel share chords and differ in words, then recalls summers in North Carolina with her grandmother and the moaner's bench.

story.theme_name: Church, faith and religion in a musician's life
story.community_name: Church, faith and jazz: the sacred and the secular

blocks.x: Yes. And I try to share that. I teach History of Jazz class and I try to share those things. I want to ask you something now about rhythm & blues as compared to Gospel. People say it’s the same chords. It’s the same beat. One person said it’s like the only difference is one guy’s talking about God and one guy’s talking about his girlfriend.
There you go, it’s just changing the words.
Give us an example of a couple that were close.

You know what you say is very true and I find myself having to watch that when you do Gospel, and especially the now generation Gospel. I have to really closely listen to what’s being said, you know, to kind of slow down and respect the fact that they’re singing Gospel. Unlike when I came along, my father was Baptist, was Methodist. My mother was Baptist. So I was christened as a Methodist as a baby, and I sang in that choir when I became of age. But each summer when I had to work in the fields in cotton and tobacco, I was sent to North Carolina. My mother’s people were Baptist. My grandmother refused to accept the fact that by having a few speckles of water dropped on my head that that meant anything spiritually. And so consequently we were required to go to the moaner’s bench. The moaner’s bench. You had to sit there. The whole month of August was the viable month. So you went to church in the morning, if you were a sinner as the deacons called you, you sat on that moaner’s bench while the older deacons walked around you and admonished you for not having received God, you see? And if and when you did you stood up and shouted. And of course we sat there so long that my sisters and I decided we were just going to hop up. We had just rehearsed our chorus before we left the house one day, we were tired of sitting there. So we hopped up at a given moment, like the Rockettes, we’d be with legs hopping and everything. Of course my grandmother had a very keen eye. And she saw all of this. And she just gave us one look, you know in those days all they had to do was give you a look, and didn’t have to say anything —
And just peak over the glasses.
